<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and stayed disciplined about evidence, but A built the clearer decision rule: a headline target must be single, falsifiable, and beyond the government's power to rewrite. A's "name the number" question extracted the pivotal concession ("There is no single figure, and the motion does not require one"), then exploited it well — if the domains diverge, someone chooses the headline, and B's own answer conceded the legislature (i.e. the governing majority) fixes the domains, letting the examined body write its own exam. A also answered B's strongest counter-pressure squarely: GDP's narrowness is why it cannot launder health failures as "balance," with specific biting instruments (safety law, emissions caps, real wages, mortality data) doing the work B assigned to a composite. B's reframe of "primary" as governing priority was legitimate and its central question — which failures must policy answer for? — remained live to the end, and it correctly noted GDP does not abolish political judgment. But B's case stayed abstract, offered no concrete illustrations to rival A's Southern European unemployment and UK stagnation examples, and never neutralized the enforceability objection beyond "outsiders can complain." A also framed the stakes more memorably ("a target you cannot miss is not a target"; "keep the leash short") in ways tied to real argument rather than decoration. A pays a modest execution cost for two turns clipped over the word limit, which trims the margin.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Pressure Question "name the number," and its follow-up handling of B's concession: once B admitted there is no single figure and that the legislature fixes the domains, A converted that into the twin charges that "primary" does no work and that the government writes its own examination — the exchange B never fully recovered from.</best_rebuttal>
